IMAGE ROLES:
1. source room — the only authority for architecture, camera and room proportions

TASK
Create a photorealistic, aspirational editorial photograph of the SAME bedroom after a cosmetic renovation in the selected style.
This is not a new room and not a deep structural renovation. The room volume, architecture and camera must remain identical to the source. Change only surface finishes, furniture, lighting, textiles, decor and styling.
The result must feel like a completed designer renovation with a genuine WOW effect: the kind of image that makes the viewer want to live in this room and save it to a Pinterest board. It must not look like a moodboard, a sterile furniture showroom or an empty staged flat.
This is the art-direction pass. Design the strongest room first; do not turn the image into a catalog assembly. Specific hero products can be attached later in separate local edits.

ARCHITECTURE LOCK — HIGHEST PRIORITY
This is the SAME physical room from the source photograph, captured by the same camera. Recreate that exact room with new finishes.
PRESERVE EXACTLY:
- Camera: the same position, eye height, focal length, perspective, horizon, framing, crop and aspect ratio. The left/right and top/bottom composition stays identical.
- Room volume: the same width, depth, ceiling height, wall planes, floor plane, soffits, beams, columns, niches and arches.
- Windows: the same count, size, shape, position, sill, reveal, frame, glazing bars and radiator niche.
- Doors: the same count, size, position, frame, handle and swing.
- Built-ins are architecture, not furniture: built-in wardrobes, mirrored wardrobes, kitchen cabinets, shelving, niches, wall panels, banquettes, media walls and radiator grilles. Keep their exact footprint, depth, height, bay divisions, shelf spacing and vertical dividers.
- Electrical: the exact position of every visible outlet, switch, ceiling light point, radiator, pipe, vent, TV and wall-mounted item. New lights use only the existing points.
- Floor: keep the existing plank or tile direction, pattern, seams and board width; change only the surface colour and finish.
- Mirrors and reflections stay reflections; the only room they reflect is the existing room.
- If a design idea conflicts with any locked element, keep the architecture and change the finish, furniture or decor instead.

ART DIRECTION — BESPOKE FOR THIS ROOM
Written by the art director from the source photo. Follow it for palette, materials, focal point, lighting, textiles and styling. If it conflicts with the ARCHITECTURE LOCK or the scale plan, keep the architecture and the real dimensions.
A serene, warm Scandinavian bedroom designed with natural oak and tactile linen. The room features a low-profile bed with organic rounded forms, anchoring the space. A feature wall behind the bed uses a muted sage paint combined with soft stucco texture. The palette is dominated by light oak, creamy off-whites, and deep terracotta accents. Layered lighting includes a large woven pendant over the sleeping area and warm floor lamps, creating soft shadows. The floor is covered with a large, textured wool rug. Curated decor consists of handmade ceramic vessels and a single large abstract painting in muted tones, establishing a balanced, grounded, and exceptionally peaceful atmosphere.


BED SIZE — MANDATORY
Include a bed with an overall external length of exactly 2 metres, measured from the head end to the foot end, including its frame. This measurement refers to the whole bed, not just the mattress.
The bed width is not specified. Choose a width appropriate to the room’s layout and available circulation space.
Keep the bed realistically proportioned. Do not shorten, stretch or visually compress it to make the arrangement fit. Avoid an oversized headboard or footboard that increases the overall bed length beyond 2 metres.

RADIATOR COVERS — REQUIRED WHEN RADIATORS ARE PRESENT
If any heating radiators are visible in Image 1, visually conceal each of them behind a purpose-designed decorative radiator cover. Keep the actual radiator and heating connections in their original positions. Do not remove, relocate or replace the heating system.
Design the covers as understated elements coordinated with the room’s palette, materials and selected style:
- Clean, simple proportions.
- A visually lightweight, slatted or perforated front.
- Warm off-white, a matching wall colour or a suitable natural-wood appearance.
Use one coherent cover design throughout the room.
Show a clearly ventilated construction:
- An open grille, spaced slats or substantial perforations at the front.
- An unobstructed lower air inlet.
- A continuous upper grille or open outlet for rising warm air.
Do not create a sealed box or a solid cabinet that visually traps the radiator behind an unventilated surface.
Keep thermostatic valve heads and controls accessible and outside the enclosed warm-air pocket. Do not depict an ordinary thermostatic valve head sealed inside the cover.
Make the front panel appear removable for maintenance. Allow plausible clearance around the radiator without inventing precise installation dimensions.
Keep the cover proportionate to the existing radiator. Do not extend it into a full wall of cabinetry or an oversized bench. Do not add upholstered seating, cushions or storage on top.
Where the radiator is beneath a window:
- Preserve the window’s dimensions and original position.
- Keep the cover below the window opening.
- Do not obstruct window operation.
- Do not cover the upper ventilation outlet with curtains or objects.
Do not cover separate wall ventilation grilles or air vents. Do not invent radiators or radiator covers where none are present.
These covers are part of the visual design concept, not a technical installation specification.

KEEP EXACTLY
the bed, bedside tables, wardrobe and their realistic proportions; the architecture, camera, walls, windows, doors and ceiling height. Keep the bed functional and do not block doors or windows.
Keep the room purpose exactly as a bedroom. Do not move plumbing, electrical points, windows or doors.

FURNITURE MODE
Preserve existing large furniture and functional zones. Restyle or replace in place; do not move pieces aligned with outlets, radiators or built-ins; do not swap sides or rearrange the room. Built-ins and mirror panels are architecture and must stay.

FURNITURE PLACEMENT
Keep the existing functional zones and furniture positions. The bed stays against the same wall with the same headboard orientation; do not center it under the window if it was not there. Desk/wardrobe/sofa stay in the same zones, TV stays on the same wall. Restyle or replace furniture in place; do not swap sides, move across the room or block the window/door. If a piece is aligned with outlets, radiators or built-ins, keep its position.

CHANGE / DEEP TRANSFORMATION
Update surface finishes, textiles, lighting and decor without changing the room layout..
If a floor product is listed below, change only its surface finish; do not change the floor plane or geometry. If no floor product is listed, preserve the existing floor. Style words such as "light oak" refer to furniture and joinery only, not to replacing the floor unless a floor product is explicitly listed. The same applies to walls: change only the surface finish when a wall finish is listed.
Keep the result functional, keep realistic dimensions, and do not block doors or windows.

COMPOSITION
Keep the camera and architecture. Create a strong focal point, balanced composition and believable depth. Freestanding furniture may be moved only when furniture replacement is allowed; built-ins, plumbing and electrical points stay in place. No distorted geometry, no floating objects, no duplicate furniture.

LIGHTING DESIGN — THE MAIN WOW TOOL
Use only the existing electrical points and ceiling/wall positions. Do not add new ceiling recesses, coves, tracks, wall-wash fixtures, sconces, niches or second pendant points. If a cove already exists in the source, a subtle warm LED strip is allowed; otherwise keep the ceiling plane flat. Use warm 2700–3000K light, layered with existing fixtures and plug-in lamps. No new architectural lighting, no boob lights, no cold white light, no visible bulbs or dangling wires. Choose the fixture for the interior composition; do not copy a fixture from an art reference or catalog card.

CLEANUP / REALISM
Remove visual noise: old TVs, cable boxes, exposed wires, dangling cables, window air conditioners, old chandeliers, old wall art, cheap plastic blinds, old roller blinds, torn or yellowed curtains, clutter and visible meters. Keep the window sill, the wall plane under the window, the radiator niche and all built-ins exactly as they are. Replace only the radiator body with a flush wall-colored grille of the same size; never remove the niche or change the wall. Keep built-in wardrobes, mirrored wardrobe, kitchen cabinets, shelving and niches. If a TV remains, mount it flush with hidden cables or use a frame TV; otherwise remove it. No visible cables anywhere.

WINDOW STYLING
Replace old blinds and curtains with new treatments that hang from the existing ceiling/wall line. Do not raise, widen, lower or move the window opening; do not add a cornice niche or alter the ceiling line. Use floor-length curtains, linen sheers or a clean Roman/roller blind. Never keep cheap plastic horizontal or vertical blinds, torn curtains or a bare window unless the style explicitly calls for it. No new window.

ROOM RULES
A comfortable bed with an upholstered headboard, two bedside tables, soft textiles, a wardrobe and calm layered lighting are appropriate. No kitchen, no sink/faucet, no toilet, shower or bathroom fixtures, no kitchen cabinets or countertop, no large-format porcelain floor tile. The floor must stay wood, laminate, carpet or vinyl unless a floor product explicitly says otherwise.

LIFE & STYLING — THIS IS WHERE THE WOW EFFECT COMES FROM
Add tasteful textiles, art, plants, books, ceramics and warm layered lighting; make it feel finished and lived-in. All decor must stay inside the existing wall, floor and ceiling planes. Use only existing shelves, ledges and niches; never add a new built-in, ledge, cove or wall panel.
Add generous but tasteful small details: layered textiles, cushions, throws, curtains, rugs, framed art, books, ceramics, candles, trays, plants and sculptural objects. All decor must sit inside the existing room volume; do not alter wall, floor or ceiling planes, corners, perspective, plinth or room proportions. Use warm layered lighting — ceiling, bedside/floor lamps, cove and accent light — with soft shadows and tactile material contrast. Layer soft textures and warm pools of light. The room must feel cozy, inhabited, warm, calm and aspirational, like a boutique hotel suite or a designer portfolio. Never a bare mattress, empty walls or a cold showroom.

PINTEREST-LEVEL STYLING
Make it look like a saved Pinterest reference: fully furnished, curated, layered and personal, with 3–5 styled vignettes rather than random clutter. Do not leave the room empty or half-finished. Add art only on existing wall planes, shelves only on existing ledges or freestanding within the room; do not add niches, ledges, wall panels, beams, columns or new built-ins. MUST INCLUDE at least one art grouping (2–4 frames) or one large poster, a styled surface using existing shelves/console/ledge or a freestanding table, floor-length curtains or a clean blind, and layered textiles (throw, cushions or rug). Do not add a new shelf, ledge or niche. Textiles: floor-length curtains, throws, cushions, rugs, table runners. Walls: framed art, posters, a small gallery wall, textile panel or wall hanging. Shelves: open shelving with books, ceramics, vases, candles, small sculptures, records and plants. Personal objects: a modern laptop (MacBook-style), headphones, a speaker, a camera, magazines. Place them on a desk, nightstand, console, shelf, coffee table or bed — never on the floor or rug. A laptop may be open on a desk or closed on a nightstand/console. Hide chargers, cables, camera straps and loose wires. Plush toys: only in a children's room or a bedroom, one or two, styled on a chair, bed or shelf — never on the floor. Never in bathrooms, kitchens or adult living rooms. Keep it tasteful and uncluttered: every object should look intentional, not scattered. The scene must feel personal and collected, not like a furniture showroom.


CATALOG / MATERIALS
The listed products are the material palette. The estimate is built from them.

MATERIAL CONSTRAINTS — TEXT ONLY, NO PRODUCT IMAGES
1. floor finish: Инженерная доска «Светлый дуб» — floor [цвет: светлый дуб, материал: инженерная доска, покрытие: матовая] (no reference image — use the described color/finish only)
2. wall finish: Краска «Жемчужный беж» — paint [цвет: тёплый беж, блеск: матовая, основа: водоэмульсионная] (no reference image — use the described color/finish only)
3. skirting boards: Плинтус «Дуб, шпон» — skirting [цвет: натуральный дуб, высота: 80 мм, материал: шпон] (no reference image — use the described color/finish only)
4. sockets and switches: Розетки «Белые, классика» — outlets [цвет: белый, рамка: скрытая, материал: пластик] (no reference image — use the described color/finish only)
Use these text descriptions only as constraints for finishes, colors, formats and physical scale. Match large surfaces (floor, walls, countertop, cabinet fronts) to the listed material where visible. Tile/plank patterns must match the stated format. Do not force a material into the frame if it is not visible. Choose furniture, lighting, decor and composition for the strength of the design rather than trying to depict the estimate. Small decor, plants, textiles, art and books are encouraged to complete the styling.

STYLE BRIEF
Warm, characterful, designer-led Scandinavian interior.

DESIGN DIRECTION:
Create a contemporary Scandinavian interior with warm natural materials,
a restrained but expressive palette, functional furniture and curated details.
Balance clean lines with soft forms, craftsmanship and a lived-in atmosphere.
Use the existing room size realistically; do not overcrowd the space.

COLOUR PALETTE:
Use warm off-white, oatmeal and natural oak as the foundation.
Introduce muted sage or dusty blue as a clearly visible secondary colour,
supported by small touches of terracotta or rust.
Use charcoal sparingly for visual definition.
Repeat the selected accent colour in two or three deliberate places.
Avoid an entirely white, grey or beige room.

WALL COMPOSITION:
Give the main visible wall an intentional design treatment.
Choose ONE coherent approach appropriate to the room:
- a muted sage or dusty-blue painted wall with one oversized artwork;
- a warm off-white wall with a carefully composed group of two or three substantial framed prints;
- a restrained colour-block treatment with a large graphic artwork.
Scale artwork to the furniture and available wall area.
Do not leave the main wall visually unresolved.
Retain some calm negative space; do not decorate every wall.
Avoid tiny scattered pictures, arbitrary panels and excessive ornament.

FURNITURE:
Use well-proportioned Scandinavian furniture with functional forms,
slender or gently rounded profiles, and visible natural wood.
Combine light oak or ash with tactile upholstery.
Create one clear focal point appropriate to the room’s function.
Introduce one distinctive piece, such as a sculptural lounge chair,
a colourful upholstered chair or a characterful wooden cabinet.
Avoid making every piece identical in material, colour or silhouette.
Maintain believable furniture dimensions and usable circulation paths.

MATERIALS AND TEXTURES:
Create a coherent combination of natural oak or ash, wool or a textured woven rug,
linen or cotton textiles, matte painted surfaces, ceramics and small details
in brushed metal or dark metal. Make the textures visibly distinct but harmonious.
Avoid glossy plastic-looking surfaces and excessive bouclé.

LIGHTING:
Combine soft natural daylight with a believable layered lighting scheme.
Use a pendant or ceiling fixture suited to the existing room,
a floor or reading lamp, and a small table lamp where appropriate.
Prefer warm, softly diffused artificial light around 2700–3000 K.
Place lamps logically near seating, reading or working areas.
Do not rely only on ceiling downlights.
Do not invent architectural recesses or concealed ceiling lighting.

TEXTILES:
Use a generously sized textured rug appropriate to the furniture grouping.
Add a restrained combination of cushions and a casually placed throw.
Use natural-fabric curtains where the window arrangement allows,
without obscuring radiators, doors or essential access.
Mix plain textiles with one subtle stripe, check or graphic pattern.

DECOR AND PERSONALITY:
Style the room with a small number of deliberate, well-scaled objects:
a substantial artwork, ceramic vessels, a few books, a sculptural object
and one plant where space and daylight allow.
Arrange objects in intentional groupings rather than scattering them everywhere.
Make the room feel inhabited and personal, not staged with random accessories.
Keep functional surfaces usable.

COMPOSITION:
Establish one primary focal point and a few supporting details.
Balance wood, textiles, colour and open space.
Create visual interest through proportion, contrast, texture and asymmetry,
not through excessive decoration.
Keep the result achievable in a real home.

AVOID:
Bare unresolved main walls, an all-white or all-grey palette,
generic showroom styling, oversized furniture, random clutter,
excessive plants, tiny scattered decor, cold blue lighting,
distorted furniture, new architectural openings and changes to the room geometry.

STYLE REFERENCE
There is no separate style reference. Build the photographic language from the style description, room and material constraints.
The art reference is for palette, materials and light temperature ONLY. Ignore all architecture in the reference: windows, doors, sloped ceilings, niches, bay windows, beams, room size, layout and camera. Do not transfer any architectural feature from the reference.


MATERIAL CLASS
Comfort — balanced mid-range materials: engineered wood, quartz or compact countertops, quality painted or veneered cabinetry, warm brass or steel fixtures, layered lighting.
The selected materials already match this class; keep the rest of the room consistent with it.

OUTPUT
Photorealistic editorial interior photograph, 24–35mm wide angle, natural window light or warm golden hour, soft shadows, subtle film grain, realistic color grading, medium-format look, high detail, 8k. It must look like a real photograph, not a 3D render or CGI. No text, no watermarks, no people, no new windows, no extra windows, no resized windows, no new doors, no new doorways, no new walls, no widened room, no changed ceiling height, no new niches, no new beams, no new columns, no new skylights, no new room, no changed camera, no changed perspective, no moved radiator, no moved outlets, no duplicated shelves, no warped shelves, no duplicated furniture, no distorted geometry, no cartoon or CGI look, no bare mattress, no empty walls, no sterile showroom feeling, no visible radiator panel, no exposed radiators, no old TV with dangling cables, no generic chandelier, no mismatched light fixtures, no cold flat lighting, no random clutter, no old electronics, no electronics on the floor or rug, no loose cables, chargers or camera straps, no plush toys in bathrooms or kitchens, no old plastic blinds, no torn curtains, no empty shelves.
